query: Earlier empirical-potential and first-principles studies primarily targeted phase-transition temperature, while other fusion properties remain difficult because they require free energies on both sides of the transition with vibrational entropy, anharmonicity, and electron–vibration coupling retained. Explicit ab initio free-energy evaluation is highly accurate but depends on costly molecular dynamics. TOR-TILD increased throughput for elemental and binary systems, yet slows substantially for multicomponent high-entropy systems. Under the constraint that the free energies of both solid and fluid states and the relevant entropy terms remain faithful, what single testable methodological hypothesis could substantially reduce the cost of obtaining fusion and high-temperature thermodynamic properties? State the proposed intervention and why it should work, predict its speed and fidelity relative to explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics workflows and TOR-TILD, define composition and temperature boundaries, cite supporting evidence from prior elemental or binary results, and specify a decisive benchmark of phase free energies and derived observables that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: An actively learned, data‐driven ML potential framework can substantially reduce the cost of obtaining fusion and high-temperature thermodynamic properties by accurately capturing the free energy landscapes of both solid and fluid states (including vibrational entropy, anharmonicity, and electron–vibration coupling) without exhaustive ab initio MD simulations.
generation.material_initial_state: Elemental, binary, and multicomponent (high-entropy) alloys near their fusion temperatures.
generation.intervention: Implement an active learning ML potential method that iteratively refines its predictions with sparse ab initio data, thereby building an accurate surrogate for the free energies of both solid and liquid states.
generation.conditions: High-temperature conditions around the melting point, applicable to systems ranging from simple elemental and binary alloys to complex high-entropy alloys.
generation.structural_mediator: The ML potential will incorporate key structural descriptors that capture vibrational, anharmonic, and electron–vibration coupling effects, ensuring that the surrogate model faithfully represents both phases’ free energy landscapes.
generation.mechanism: By using an active learning approach, initial ab initio MD data are used to train an ML surrogate that is iteratively refined. This minimizes the number of costly ab initio evaluations while retaining sufficient fidelity in the free energy predictions across states and compositions.
generation.predicted_outcome: A substantial reduction in computational cost (potentially an order-of-magnitude improvement over full ab initio MD) while maintaining free energy accuracy comparable to state-of-the-art methods such as TOR-TILD in elemental and binary systems, with extended applicability to high-entropy systems.
generation.baseline: Explicit ab initio free-energy calculations via molecular dynamics and the TOR-TILD method, which are accurate but computationally expensive, especially for multicomponent alloys.
generation.boundary: The method is expected to be effective over compositional ranges from pure elements to high-entropy alloys and for temperatures spanning from just below the fusion point up to complete melting.
generation.uncertainty: While evidence from elemental and binary systems supports the potential of ML surrogates, the fidelity of the approach and its scaling to highly multicomponent high-entropy systems remains to be definitively verified.

falsification_experiment.design: Develop and benchmark the active learning ML potential for a set of materials that includes an elemental system, a binary alloy, and a high-entropy alloy. For each system, compute the free energy curves for both solid and liquid states near the fusion transition using the ML potential and compare to explicit ab initio MD results.
measurements: Free energy differences between solid and liquid phases
Predicted vibrational entropy and anharmonicity metrics
Total computational time required for the ML framework vs. full ab initio MD
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the active learning ML potential fails to reproduce the phase free energies within an acceptable error margin (e.g., >5% deviation) or does not reduce the computational cost by at least an order-of-magnitude relative to ab initio MD, particularly for high-entropy alloys, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractExploring the vast compositional space offered by multicomponent systems or high entropy materials using the traditional route of materials discovery, one experiment at a time, is prohibitive in terms of cost and required time. Consequently, the development of high‐throughput experimental methods, aided by machine learning and theoretical predictions will facilitate the search for multicomponent materials in their compositional variety. In this study, high entropy oxides are fabricated and characterized using automated high‐throughput techniques. For intuitive visualization, a graphical phase–property diagram correlating the crystal structure, the chemical composition, and the band gap are introduced. Interpretable machine learning models are trained for automated data analysis and to speed up data comprehension. The establishment of materials libraries of multicomponent systems correlated with their properties (as in the present work), together with machine learning‐based data analysis and theoretical approaches are opening pathways toward virtual development of novel materials for both functional and structural applications. To speed up the data analysis, we developed an adaptable and highly interpretable machine learning approach. This approach is capable of determining, in a shorter amount of time, whether an X‐ray diffractogram is representative of a pure single phase or whether there are multiple phases present in a sample and thus providing intuitive explanations for the prediction (further details are provided in the experimental section). An example of the predictive power of the approach is illustrated for the multi‐phase sample (Sm0.5Y0.5)O2− δ , along with an explanation why the ML models classifies it as multi‐phase, as shown in Figure 4a (further examples in Section 5, Supporting Information). A second machine learning model, trained directly on the materials compositions in the experimental dataset, was used to obtain feature importance values that are interpretable as well. In this section, we discuss the results of the development of the interatomic-potential model used to enable the application of MD simulations of dislocation properties in bcc MoNbTaW. We employ the general framework of machine-learning (ML)-based approaches, which have emerged recently as a systematic framework to develop potentials with accuracies near that of the underlying DFT calculations for elemental and multicomponent systems,. Here, using training data reported previously for elemental, binary, ternary, and quaternary systems in Nb–Ta–Mo–W, we developed a potential for the MoNbTaW RHEA based on the moment tensor potential (MTP) formalism, which has been found to feature an excellent balance between accuracy and computational cost. The flowchart for constructing the MTP is shown in Fig. 1a with the methodological details provided in “Methods”. The basic materials property predictions of the MTP model are provided in Supplementary Table 1.
